newsitem.title: UK: UN mulls price cut for Iraq crude to Europe - traders.
newsitem.headline: UN mulls price cut for Iraq crude to Europe - traders.

text.p: The United Nations is considering a request from oil traders to cut the price of Iraq's Kirkuk Blend crude by 20-25 cents a barrel for European customers because of deteriorating spot market values, oil traders said on Friday.
"The proposal is for a downward adjustment of 20-25 cents a barrel for the second half of March and the whole of April," said a lifter of Iraqi crude.
"It is coming from traders who are finding it impossible to sell Kirkuk in the Mediterranean but it will also have the support of the refiners," he added.

Kirkuk Blend, exported to Europe via the Turkish port of Ceyhan under the terms of the U.N.'s oil-for-food deal implemented last December, is currently priced for March at benchmark Dated Brent less $1.55.
Kirkuk, linked to changes in the value of Saudi Arab Light, would be priced at Brent less $1.65 for April after a 10-cent Saudi reduction for the month.

But with Russian Urals crude, Kirkuk's main rival grade in the key Mediterranean spot market, currently priced at about Dated Brent less $1.20, traders say it is impossible to find buyers for the Iraqi barrels.
"At the current level it is not attractive at all," said a trader.
"A lot of Kirkuk is in traders hands and they are losing about 20-25 cents a barrel at the moment because they don't have a refining system to put it into," he said.

European lifters of Iraqi crude oil said the proposal for an increase in the discount, which would price Kirkuk at Dated Brent less $1.75-$1.80 for the balance of March and Dated less $1.85-$1.90 for April, was the only way to ensure traders lift all their contracted volumes.
"The proposal is being considered by the U.N. overseers (of the oil-for-food deal) at the moment -- it is not official yet," said a trader at a European refiner.
Last month, the U.N. sanctions committee on Iraq approved deeper discounts for Iraqi crude sales to the U.S., trimming the price of U.S.-bound Basrah Light in March by 20 cents a barrel.
European traders said SOMO's U.S. customers may be looking for even bigger discounts.
